title: Helix Toolbox
summary: Set up and look after a Linux machine from one menu in the terminal.
text: Linux setup Applications, dotfiles and shell configuration, system tweaks, updates, backups and health checks. Every change is planned, shown with its risk, confirmed, verified and recorded. Linux on x86_64 or aarch64 with glibc 2.35 or later. Tested on Arch, Debian, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, Fedora and openSUSE Tumbleweed. A catalog of hundreds of applications and tweaks, with profiles and a first-run wizard for developer, gaming, privacy and minimal setups. Knows your machine: what is installed and from where (pacman, apt, dnf, zypper, AUR, Flatpak), its version and any waiting updates. The Install Plan shows every step, its risk and any password prompt, and checks conflicts, repositories, hardware and disk space before anything runs. Runs are verified, fall back from the AUR to Flathub when they need to, and land in a history you can read later. Helix Doctor checks the system and offers repairs, which you confirm one by one. Snapshots with Snapper or Timeshift, and Restic backups that are test-restored and checked against SHA-256 sums. Drift checks, moving a setup between distributions, firmware and hardware health, systemd services, Git repositories and Home Manager generations. A Ctrl-K command palette, a desktop window, and a command line where everything takes --dry-run and --json.

title: Helix Boot
summary: A multiboot rescue USB that builds itself from upstream sources.
text: Recovery Current tools, verified downloads, a boot menu you can theme, and room for your own licensed software. Recovery, diagnostics and repair on one stick. Builds sticks on Windows and Linux; macOS can update an existing stick. Built on Ventoy, PhoenixPE and PortableApps.com. Always current: every tool resolves to its latest upstream release each time you refresh. Verified: downloads are checked against the publisher’s checksum or GitHub’s digest, and anything without one is refused unless you trust it explicitly. Free tools by default, with slots for paid tools you bring yourself. Nothing is redistributed. Refresh updates the stick in place and keeps files you added; check reads it back for damaged files. Seven boot-menu themes, icon styles and your own background and splash, previewed before they are written. Offline packs: the whole stick in one zip that builds a new stick with no internet. Lazarus PE: your own Windows 11 PE with a full-screen tool launcher. Only USB disks are offered, and the device is checked again before each write.

title: Config Bible
summary: A handbook for your own workstation, with search, in a web site and a desktop app.
text: Documentation One folder of Markdown pages behind two viewers: a searchable web site and a desktop app with a command palette, live reload and pages you can mark as checked. Linux. The desktop app is a Tauri app, packaged for Arch. The same Markdown source behind a MkDocs Material site and a desktop app. A Ctrl-K command palette, search across the handbook, find on page, back and forward, breadcrumbs, pins, recent pages, tags and backlinks. Live reload: an edited page shows without a rebuild. Open a page in Neovim, jump to the file it describes, or mark it verified today. Checks every page’s metadata, links and code blocks, so stale pages stand out. Colors follow your desktop theme.

title: webOS Launcher
summary: A minimal home screen for LG webOS TVs.
text: TV Favorites, Plex rows, inputs, moving themes and a screensaver, made for a stock TV in Developer Mode (webOS 5 and later). Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. An LG TV with webOS 5 or later in Developer Mode, or rooted with Homebrew Channel. Node.js 20 or later on a computer on the same network. Weather and clock, a Favorites row, and recently used apps on rooted TVs. Plex rows: Continue Watching, Recently Added, and Watchlist on rooted TVs. All Apps you can rearrange and hide. Inputs show only what is plugged in, named after the device. Themes: Ambient, Aurora, Midnight, Ocean, Sunset and Starry space, or your own picture or video wallpaper. Icons as the apps ship them, or glass tiles in white, brand color or ice blue. A screensaver with clock and weather over your photos and videos, or Plex art. Syncs and updates itself every hour. On rooted TVs: a phone remote page, commercial mute, layout backup and app updates.

title: Touchdown
summary: Live NFL scores and stats in your terminal.
text: Game day A keyboard-driven dashboard for game day: live, final and upcoming games, your team’s season at a glance, and a game center with box scores and play-by-play. Linux, macOS and Windows. Prebuilt binaries come with SHA-256 sums; building needs Go 1.24 or later. A scores dashboard with live, final and upcoming games, a card for your team, and standings on wide terminals. Your team’s view: next matchup, latest result, bye week, schedule, record and stat leaders. A game center with box scores, player stats, play-by-play, quarter scores, scoring plays and drives. Follow any team, in one of three themes: mint, amber or mono. Optional desktop alerts when your team scores. Keeps working offline from cached results, marked as cached. td -once prints the scores once and exits, for scripts and status bars.

title: Inside Helix Toolbox: one Linux setup tool, in the terminal or on the desktop
summary: What Helix Toolbox does, how a run works from plan to history, how the terminal and desktop versions compare, and how to install it or try it in one command.
text: Linux setup Guides Setting up a Linux machine means a long list of small jobs: install the applications you use, add the right repositories, set up your shell, turn on backups, check that nothing is broken. A few weeks later the machine needs updates from three different package tools, and you can't remember what you changed. Helix Toolbox puts those jobs in one place. It works whether this is your first Linux machine or your fiftieth, and it never changes anything until it has shown you what it's about to do. What it is, in plain words Helix Toolbox is a free, open source program for setting up and looking after a Linux machine. It covers applications, dotfiles and shell configuration, system tweaks, updates, backups and health checks. You pick what you want from a catalog of nearly 300 entries. It works out the steps, shows them to you with their risk, runs them once you confirm, checks that they worked and keeps a record. It's written in Rust, it's MIT licensed, and it works the same way on Arch, Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora and openSUSE. Distributions built on those use the same package managers. Every change is tested in containers of each of them, with real package installs and removals. If you're new to Linux, the important part is that you don't need to know the commands first. If you've been at this for years, the appeal is different: one view of every package tool on the machine, and plans you can read before they run. Terminal or desktop There are two ways to use it, and both are the same program underneath. - The terminal interface runs with helix-toolbox , or htb for short. You can use it over SSH, and it works with the keyboard or the mouse. - The desktop window runs with helix-toolbox-gui and opens from your application menu like any other program. The dashboard in the terminal and in the desktop window. The window shows the same catalog, keeps the same Install Plan, and makes the same checks before a run, with the same confirmation, verification and history. The run itself happens in a terminal embedded in the window, so you still see every line of output. Every change to the machine goes through the same engine, whichever one you started from. The Applications screen in each. The window shows the selected entry's details beside the list. So the choice comes down to where you like to work. If you're a beginner, start with the window. If you live in a terminal or manage a machine over SSH, use the terminal interface. You don't have to settle on one, since they share your settings and history. How a run works Every change follows the same five steps. This is the heart of Helix Toolbox. 1. Choose. Queue what you want. In the terminal, Space adds the entry you're on. In the window, tick it. 2. Plan. The Install Plan lists the steps in order, what each one needs, its risk, and whether it will ask for your password. It checks for conflicts, missing repositories, the wrong hardware and too little disk space before anything runs. 3. Confirm. Nothing happens until you say so. 4. Verify. Installs and removals are checked against the package manager afterward. If a source fails, it falls back to the next one: the AUR, then Flathub. 5. Record. Every run, its output and its result are kept in History, so you can read later what happened. The Install Plan, before anything runs. The window asks the same question: here is the risk, here are the steps, and here is what each one changes. Want to look closer? In the terminal interface, p shows exactly what an entry runs, and e shows what a plan will change on this machine, with configuration files side by side as the installer would write them. It also marks what can't be known in advance. Run it as your normal user. Entries that need root ask for your password when they run. What it can do The list is long, so here are the parts most people reach for first. Applications and profiles The catalog covers applications, development tools, gaming, desktop and shell configuration, maintenance and security, in searchable groups. Each entry shows whether it's installed, where it came from (pacman, apt, dnf, zypper, the AUR or Flatpak), which version you have, and whether an update is waiting. On the first start, a setup wizard looks at the machine and turns a choice of Developer, Gaming, Privacy or Minimal into an Install Plan for you to review. Press Ctrl-K at any time to reach any screen, action or entry by name. Updates in one place The Updates screen gathers what every package tool on the machine has waiting, and hands the work to those tools. You don't have to remember whether something came from your distribution, Flatpak or the AUR. Helix Doctor Helix Doctor checks the network, services, graphics drivers, package databases, permissions, boot images, GRUB, the EFI partition and disk space. Where it finds a problem it offers a repair, and each repair runs only after its own confirmation. Helix Doctor in the terminal and in the window. Snapshots and backups A Snapper or Timeshift snapshot is taken before system changes, and configuration backups can be restored from one screen. For your own files there are Restic backups, with a file's history across snapshots, restores into a new folder that overwrite nothing, backups on a timer, and recovery tests that restore a file and compare its SHA-256. A backup you've tested is one you can trust. Drift and moving between machines HELIX Drift saves how a machine is set up and shows what has moved since, or what a fresh installation still lacks, with the entries that put it back queued for review. Migration goes further: it writes what this machine has to a file that another machine or distribution can read. Catalog entries become that distribution's packages, Flatpaks come from Flathub, and any packages that don't translate are listed for you. Hardware and firmware The Hardware screen covers firmware updates through fwupd, disk, temperature and battery health, and PCI and USB devices. SMART checks and firmware updates sit behind their own confirmation. The Hardware page in the desktop window. For power users - Services and storage: systemd services and timers, the applications started at login, and where your disk space goes, with what each cleanup would free. - Repositories: the Git repositories under your project folders, with changes, branches and stashes, committed and synced through reviewed plans. - Home Manager: generations, the files it links, and build, switch and going back to a generation as reviewed plans. - Performance and recovery: how long the boot took and where the time went, and whether the machine could be brought back. - Reliability and trust: how far each entry has been tested, where an installer comes from, and what it downloads unchecked. - Offline bundles: packages, installed Flatpaks and Helix Toolbox in one checked folder, for a machine without reliable internet. Everything is also a command, with --dry-run and stable --json output, so it works in your own scripts: sh helix-toolbox search editor find entries helix-toolbox status what is installed, updated or managed helix-toolbox run git ripgrep --dry-run the plan, nothing changed helix-toolbox updates --online what every package tool has waiting helix-toolbox doctor the health checks Install it You need Linux on x86 64 or aarch64 (ARM64) with glibc 2.35 or newer. Try it without installing This runs the latest release straight from GitHub. Run it as your normal user, not with sudo : sh curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Commanderx-code/Helix-toolbox/main/start.sh sh The script downloads the release for your machine into a temporary folder, checks it against its published SHA-256 sum, runs it, and removes the folder when you quit. If you'd like to read a script before you pipe it into a shell, and that's a good habit, start.sh is short. This only tries the terminal interface. Anything you confirm inside it still happens for real. Install the terminal version Download the package for your distribution from the latest release, then run the matching command from the folder it's in. Arch, Garuda, CachyOS, EndeavourOS and Manjaro: sh sudo pacman -U helix-toolbox- -x86 64.pkg.tar.zst Debian, Ubuntu, Mint and Pop! OS: sh sudo apt install ./helix-toolbox amd64.deb Fedora: sh sudo dnf install ./helix-toolbox- .x86 64.rpm openSUSE: sh sudo zypper install --allow-unsigned-rpm ./helix-toolbox- .x86 64.rpm Any distribution, if you have Rust: sh cargo install --locked helix-toolbox On Arch there's also a package repository that keeps it updated with the rest of the system. ARM64 packages are on the same release page, and the install guide has their commands. Add the desktop window Install the terminal version above first, because the window relies on it. Then install the window's package from the same release, named helix-toolbox-gui . It comes as an Arch package, a .deb , an .rpm or an AppImage: sh sudo pacman -U helix-toolbox-gui- -x86 64.pkg.tar.zst Arch and derivatives sudo apt install ./helix-toolbox-gui amd64.deb Debian, Ubuntu sudo dnf install ./helix-toolbox-gui- .x86 64.rpm Fedora The packages add a Helix Toolbox entry to your application menu. Check your download Every release file has a SHA-256 sum and a signed build provenance attestation: sh sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS gh attestation verify <file --repo Commanderx-code/Helix-toolbox After that, you won't need to download anything by hand. The Updates screen's Helix Toolbox row fetches, checks and installs each new release, the same way your copy was installed. Your first ten minutes If this is your first time, here's a safe way to find your feet. Nothing below changes your machine until you confirm a plan. 1. Start it as your normal user, and let the setup wizard look at the machine. 2. Pick the choice closest to you and read the plan it builds. You can back out here. 3. Open Helix Doctor and see how the machine is doing. 4. Search for something you use. Press / in the terminal, or use the search field in the window. 5. Queue one small application and read its plan from top to bottom before you run it. 6. Open History afterward and see what was recorded. A few keys cover most of the terminal interface: Key Does Tab , j , k Move between screens, or within a list Enter Open a group, run an entry, or run the Install Plan Space Add the entry to the Install Plan / Search every area d Describe the entry p Show exactly what the entry runs u Update the entry Ctrl-K Find any screen, action or entry by name ? Show every key Where to go next The user guide walks through the screens and the common jobs step by step, and the window's guide covers the desktop version. If you want to know how it runs things safely, read the security notes. Found a bug or have an idea? The issue forms are open. The general catalog started as Linutil's, which is also MIT licensed, so thanks to that project too.

title: Are the tools free?
summary: Yes. Helix Toolbox, Helix Boot, webOS Launcher and Touchdown are free and open source under the MIT license. Config Bible is not public yet.

title: Which Linux distributions does Helix Toolbox work on?
summary: Linux on x86_64 or aarch64 with glibc 2.35 or later. It is tested on Arch, Debian, Ubuntu 22.04 and 24.04, Fedora and openSUSE Tumbleweed.

title: Will Helix Toolbox change my system without asking?
summary: No. The Install Plan shows every step, its risk and any password prompt before anything runs, and nothing runs until you confirm. Every command also takes --dry-run.

title: Does Helix Boot include paid software?
summary: No. It downloads free tools from their publishers and checks each one, and has slots for paid tools you bring yourself. Nothing is redistributed.

title: Could Helix Boot erase the wrong drive?
summary: It only offers USB disks, asks you to type the stick’s name to confirm, and checks the device again before each write.

title: Do I need a rooted TV for webOS Launcher?
summary: No. It runs on a stock LG TV with webOS 5 or later in Developer Mode. Rooting with Homebrew Channel adds recently used apps, the Plex Watchlist, a phone remote page, commercial mute, layout backup and app updates.

title: Does Touchdown work offline?
summary: Yes. It keeps working from cached results, and marks them as cached.

title: When will Config Bible be public?
summary: Its repository is private while the handbook is personal. Its page will link to it once it opens.

title: Something broke. Where do I report it?
summary: Each tool keeps its own issues on GitHub, and filing it there gets it fixed fastest; the contact page links to every tracker. Anything else can go through the contact form or to contact@helixstack.io.

title: Does this site track me?
summary: No. There are no cookies, no analytics and no third-party scripts. The only thing kept in your browser is the light-or-dark choice. The privacy page has the rest.
